title: High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence
author: Eric J. Topol

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Topol’s medical-domain review closely supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI shows strong but bounded task-level performance, does not establish general professional competence, and should be deployed through human-supervised workflows with rigorous, use-context-specific validation. His emphasis on prospective real-world testing and conditional rather than full automation reinforces the cluster’s case for selective deployment, verification and operating-model redesign.
qs: By the same token, medicine will unlikely ever surpass Level 3, a conditional automation, for which humans will indeed be required for oversight of algorithmic interpretation of images and data.

In summary, it is not yet known how well AI can predict key outcomes in the healthcare setting, and this will not be determined until there is robust validation in prospective, real-world clinical environments, with rigorous statistical methodology and analysis.

kp.k: Medical AI addresses data overload and systemic deficiencies
kp.d: Topol's 2019 review examines medicine rather than legal services. He argues that expanding medical data exceed human analytical capacity, while diagnostic errors, treatment mistakes, waste, workflow inefficiencies, inequities and inadequate clinician–patient time motivate AI adoption. He distinguishes emerging applications for clinicians, health systems and patients from demonstrated solutions to these longstanding problems.
qs: The limits on analysis of such data by humans alone have clearly been exceeded, necessitating an increased reliance on machines.
Yet the integration of human and artificial intelligence (AI) for medicine has barely begun.

kp.k: Benchmark accuracy does not establish clinical utility
kp.d: Topol distinguishes retrospective model performance from prospective clinical efficacy. Differences in methods prevent straightforward comparisons across studies; ROC and AUC measures may not establish usefulness, and many reports remained preprints. He calls the gap between an accurate algorithm and demonstrated improvements in outcomes the 'AI chasm'.
qs: Validation of the performance of an algorithm in terms of its accuracy is not equivalent to demonstrating clinical efficacy.
It is not possible to compare DNN accuracy from one study to the next because of marked differences in methodology.

The field clearly is far from demonstrating very high and reproducible machine accuracy, let alone clinical utility, for most medical scans and images in the real-world clinical environment (Table 1).

kp.k: Radiology results depend on tasks and evaluation conditions
kp.d: A pneumonia study using over 112,000 labeled frontal chest X-rays reported outperforming four radiologists, but Topol emphasizes its AUC of 0.76, narrow task and small comparator group. For wrist fractures, AI assistance increased sensitivity from 81% to 92% and reduced misinterpretation by 47%. A simulated prospective trial of acute neurological scans reported interpretation 150 times faster, at 1.2 versus 177 seconds, but poorer diagnostic accuracy than humans.
qs: In addition, the test used in this study is not necessarily comparable with the daily tasks of a radiologist, who will diagnose much more than pneumonia in any given scan.

It can be difficult for emergency room doctors to accurately diagnose wrist fractures, but a DNN led to marked improvement, increasing sensitivity from 81% to 92% and reducing misinterpretation by 47% (ref. 9).

kp.k: Human–AI collaboration can outperform isolated assessments
kp.d: Topol reports that a prospective breast cancer micrometastasis study involving six pathologists found the best accuracy from combined pathologist and algorithm interpretation, alongside faster slide review. He contrasts this collaborative framing with clinician-versus-machine comparisons. In an earlier retrospective comparison, pathologists' time limits materially affected results; an expert given 30 hours achieved results comparable with the algorithm.
qs: This study is particularly notable, as the synergy of the combined pathologist and algorithm interpretation was emphasized instead of the pervasive clinician-versus-algorithm comparison.
The pathologists were given 129 test slides and had less than 1 minute for review per slide, which likely does not reflect normal workflow.

kp.k: Autonomous diagnosis achieved limited prospective validation
kp.d: The review describes an IDx primary-care trial enrolling 900 patients with diabetes but no known retinopathy. Among 819 patients with analyzable images, sensitivity was 87% and specificity 91%; the trial led to FDA approval for autonomous detection of more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy. Topol emphasizes that real-world results were weaker than retrospective results and that regulation required fixing the software rather than permitting continued learning. A separate small prospective assessment produced a high false-positive rate.
qs: This trial led to FDA approval of the IDx device and algorithm for autonomous detection, that is, without the need for a clinician, of ‘more than mild’ diabetic retinopathy.
The accuracy results are not as good as the aforementioned in silico studies, which should be anticipated.

The regulatory oversight in dealing with deep-learning algorithms is tricky because it does not currently allow continued autodidactic functionality but instead necessitates fixing the software to behave like a non-AI diagnostic system30.

kp.d: Dermatology studies reported high performance, including AUCs of 0.96 for carcinoma and 0.94 for melanoma after training on nearly 130,000 images, but none occurred in clinical practice. Echocardiogram view classification achieved 92% accuracy against 79% for four specialists, although testing still images differed from reading moving video loops. In contrast, prospective colonoscopy validation in 325 patients with 466 tiny polyps reported 94% accuracy and 96% negative predictive value.
qs: None of these studies were conducted in the clinical setting, in which a doctor would perform physical inspection and shoulder responsibility for making an accurate diagnosis.
Such results are thematic: machine vision, at high magnification, can accurately and quickly interpret specific medical images as well as or better than humans.

kp.k: Algorithms may detect information beyond human perception
kp.d: Topol reports that lung-cancer pathology algorithms were trained to detect genomic driver-mutation patterns not discernible to pathologists. Retinal-image research involving over 280,000 patients achieved an AUC of 0.97 for gender, while other cardiovascular-risk-related measures were around 0.70. He treats these broader signals as potential future tools rather than established clinical benefits. He similarly presents smartwatch-based potassium detection as a prospect for obtaining previously inaccessible information without blood sampling.
qs: A deep-learning algorithm for lung cancer digital pathology slides not only was able to accurately classify tumors, but also was trained to detect the pattern of several specific genomic driver mutations that would not otherwise be discernible by pathologists33.
The potential use of retinal photographs also appears to transcend eye diseases per se.

kp.k: Outcome prediction lacks prospective proof and individual precision
kp.d: The review describes retrospective predictions of mortality, readmission, sepsis, dementia and other outcomes, including reinforcement-learning treatment recommendations for sepsis. Topol cautions that heterogeneous cohorts, incomplete inputs, overfitting risks, missing cross-validation and problematic reliance on AUC limit interpretation. Commercial marketing was already occurring despite a lack of prospective validation, and good cohort-level discrimination did not establish precise individual predictions.
qs: Both the size of the cohorts studied and the range of AUC accuracy reported have been quite heterogeneous, and all of these reports are retrospective and yet to be validated in the real-world clinical setting.
But most models are essentially classifiers and are not capable of precise prediction at the individual level, so there is still an important dimension of uncertainty.

kp.k: Workflow automation could reduce staffing requirements
kp.d: Topol identifies potential reductions in administrative work involving coding, billing, scheduling and staffing, alongside AI-assisted interpretation and documentation. He reports an estimate of processing over 250 million images daily for about $1,000 as hypothetical savings, not a demonstrated economic outcome. At Geisinger, over 100,000 patients had undergone exome sequencing, with results delivered through a chatbot reportedly reducing reliance on genetic counselors.
qs: Besides the productivity and workflow gains that can be derived from AI-assisted image interpretation and clinician support, there is potential to reduce the workforce for many types of back-office, administrative jobs such as coding and billing, scheduling of operating rooms and clinic appointments, and staffing.
This demonstrates how a health system can leverage AI tools to provide complex information without having to rely on expansion of highly trained personnel.

kp.k: Monitoring and digital twins remain prospective opportunities
kp.d: Topol describes machine vision for handwashing, intensive-care monitoring, falls, surgery and imaging improvements. He proposes wearable monitoring as a possible way to avoid hospitalization, while noting the absence of algorithmic development and prospective testing for that application at the time. He also envisages comprehensive patient datasets enabling nearest-neighbor 'digital twins', explicitly noting that patient models had not been completed at scale.
qs: Machine vision (also known as computer vision), which uses data from ambient sensors, is attracting considerable attention in health systems for promoting safety by monitoring such activities as proper clinician handwashing114, critically ill patients in the intensive care unit115, and risk of falling for patients116.

Perhaps the greatest long-term potential of AI in health systems is the development of a massive data infrastructure to support nearest-neighbor analysis, another application of AI used to identify ‘digital twins.

kp.k: Patient-facing tools combine empowerment with overdiagnosis risks
kp.d: Patient-facing AI development lagged behind clinician and health-system applications. Topol discusses smartwatch atrial-fibrillation detection, smartphone examinations, adherence monitoring, mental-health tools and individualized nutrition. He warns that screening low-risk smartwatch users could generate false positives and unnecessary evaluations. Multimodal glucose-response research provides a precedent for personalized coaching, but comprehensive virtual management of chronic disease remains a prediction.
qs: There are legitimate concerns that the widescale use of such an algorithm, particularly in the low-risk, young population who wear Apple watches, will lead to a substantial number of false-positive atrial fibrillation diagnoses and prompt unnecessary medical evalautions131.
Nevertheless, the use of AI with multimodal data to guide an individualized diet is a precedent for virtual medical coaching in the future.

kp.k: Biomedical research adopts AI faster than clinical practice
kp.d: Topol attributes faster AI progress in life sciences to easier validation, less regulatory oversight and greater willingness to implement tools. Reported applications include microscopy, rare-cell sorting, genomics, multi-omics integration, CRISPR prediction, neuroscience and drug discovery. Possible reductions in animal testing and improvements in therapy selection are presented as prospective benefits rather than established patient outcomes.
qs: While upstream from clinical practice, AI progress in life science has been notably faster, with extensive peer-reviewed publication, an easier path to validation without regulatory oversight, and far more willingness among the scientific community for implementation.
There is new hope that preclinical animal testing can be reduced via machine-learning prediction of toxicity185.

kp.k: Flawed algorithms can scale harm across institutions
kp.d: Topol uses reported problems with IBM Watson for Oncology to illustrate the danger of widespread deployment on weak evidence. He describes training based on a small number of synthetic cases and erroneous recommendations, including bevacizumab for a patient with severe bleeding. He argues that algorithmic errors can create harm on a scale beyond an individual clinician's mistake and recommends debugging, auditing, simulation and prospective validation before deployment.
qs: The state of AI hype has far exceeded the state of AI science, especially when it pertains to validation and readiness for implementation in patient care.
Instead of a single doctor’s mistake hurting a patient, the potential for a machine algorithm inducing iatrogenic risk is vast.

This is all the more reason that systematic debugging, audit, extensive simulation, and validation, along with prospective scrutiny, are required when an AI algorithm is unleashed in clinical practice.

kp.k: Transparency, inequity and security constrain implementation
kp.d: Topol describes unresolved debate over opaque neural networks, unequal access potentially widening health disparities, and embedded bias from minority underrepresentation in dermatological and genomic datasets. Privacy threats include breaches, reidentification and malicious manipulation of clinical systems. He recommends representative research, individual data rights, secure platforms and legislation; his discussion of explainability reports controversy rather than establishing a settled technical solution.
qs: Intertwined with this concern of exacerbating pre-existing inequities is embedded bias present in many algorithms due to lack of inclusion of minorities in datasets.
An overriding issue for the future of AI in medicine rests with how well privacy and security of data can be assured.

New models of health data ownership with rights to the individual, use of highly secure data platforms, and governmental legislation, as has been achieved in Estonia, are needed to counter the looming security issues that will otherwise hold up or ruin the chances for progress in AI for medicine200–202.

kp.k: Conditional automation, not clinician replacement, is the objective
kp.d: Using the self-driving-car analogy, Topol predicts that medicine is unlikely to surpass conditional automation requiring human oversight, except for routine minimal-risk matters. He advocates rigorous published studies and real-world validation before implementation. His preferred future combines complementary human and machine capabilities; anticipated gains in accuracy, productivity and workflow do not guarantee a stronger patient–doctor relationship.
qs: By the same token, medicine will unlikely ever surpass Level 3, a conditional automation, for which humans will indeed be required for oversight of algorithmic interpretation of images and data.

Accordingly, there cannot be exceptionalism for AI in medicine—it requires rigorous studies, publication of the results in peer-reviewed journals, and clinical validation in a real-world environment, before roll-out and implementation in patient care (Fig. 4).

Over time, marked improvements in accuracy, productivity, and workflow will likely be actualized, but whether that will be used to improve the patient–doctor relationship or facilitate its erosion remains to be seen.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Topol predicts that AI will transform medicine primarily through clinician augmentation, better workflow and patient self-management, rather than wholesale replacement of doctors.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about medicine, not legal services. Topol anticipates widespread clinician use of deep learning for image and data interpretation, with improvements in accuracy, speed and productivity. He presents human–machine collaboration as the principal model, while recognizing narrow autonomous applications such as diabetic-retinopathy detection. He also identifies potential substitution for administrative work and some information-delivery tasks; remote monitoring that could avert hospitalizations; individualized virtual coaching; and long-term learning systems using patients' comprehensive data and 'digital twins.' He describes AI as already accelerating biomedical research and reshaping drug discovery. These claims mix reported task-level achievements with prospective possibilities, rather than establishing general clinical or economic benefits.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Topol draws on a review of comparative studies, limited prospective clinical trials and deployment examples, distinguishing these from hypothetical savings and longer-term predictions.
pts.d: Examples include wrist-fracture assistance increasing sensitivity from 81% to 92% and reducing misinterpretation by 47%; a simulated prospective head-CT trial reporting interpretation 150 times faster than radiologists but poorer diagnostic accuracy; and a prospective pathology study in which combined pathologist–algorithm interpretation yielded the best accuracy and faster review. The IDx prospective study enrolled 900 patients and reported 87% sensitivity and 91% specificity among the 819 with analyzable images, supporting approval for autonomous detection of more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy. A prospective colonoscopy study involved 325 patients and 466 tiny polyps, with 94% accuracy and 96% negative predictive value. Topol also reports Geisinger's use of a chatbot to deliver exome-sequencing results as an example of reducing reliance on expanding specialist personnel, without supplying a quantified staffing effect. The estimate of processing more than 250 million images daily for about $1,000 is explicitly hypothetical, not demonstrated system-wide savings. Most outcome-prediction evidence reviewed is retrospective, and remote monitoring and comprehensive digital-twin systems remain proposed possibilities.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Writing in January 2019, Topol describes clinical AI as nascent and gives no fixed timetable for broad transformation; benefits depend on prospective validation, implementation and safeguards.
pts.d: The review principally discusses developments through 2018. Topol places major productivity improvements, virtual coaching and comprehensive patient-data learning systems in an unspecified future, warning that meaningful convergence is further away than many forecasts suggest. He requires rigorous studies, peer-reviewed publication and real-world clinical validation before implementation. Qualifications include narrow task definitions in clinician comparisons, unrepresentative workflows, the difference between cohort discrimination and individual prediction, inadequate data and validation, and regulatory restrictions on continued algorithm learning. Privacy, security, transparency, bias and equitable access may constrain adoption. Routine, minimally risky tasks are potential exceptions to his expectation of continuing human oversight.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are clinicians, health systems, administrative and specialist support workers, patients and biomedical researchers; benefits and risks may be unevenly distributed.
pts.d: Clinicians across specialties and paramedics may receive faster interpretation and decision support while retaining oversight responsibilities. Health systems may gain workflow efficiency, better resource allocation and potentially lower costs; administrative staff and some specialist information-delivery roles may face reduced demand. Patients may gain self-monitoring, earlier detection, personalized guidance and care outside hospital, but false positives can trigger unnecessary evaluation. Topol warns that flawed algorithms can cause harm at scale, that data breaches and attacks threaten patients, and that unequal access and underrepresentation in training data may worsen existing health inequities. Biomedical scientists and pharmaceutical developers may gain faster analysis, discovery and experimental workflows. Whether efficiency gains strengthen or erode patient–doctor relationships remains explicitly unresolved.
